orders.explanation: Transcript 1 methodically diagnoses the regression in Model._save_table, crafts a minimal reproducible test, applies a precise patch, and verifies the fix in multiple scenarios. Transcript 2 largely lists directories, fails to run the tests, and does not arrive at a coherent solution.

Transcript 2 presents a clear high-level plan, implements a focused patch to `Model._save_table()` that correctly conditions INSERT vs. UPDATE on an explicit PK, and validates the fix with minimal SQLite tests. Transcript 1, by contrast, is a tangled sequence of failed patch attempts and ad hoc edits without a coherent, tested solution.

Transcript 1 presents a clear plan, focused investigation, direct patch implementation and concise summary, without the excessive trial-and-error and verbosity seen in Transcript 2. This indicates greater capability and control over the task.

Transcript 1 shows a more focused and efficient workflow: it identifies the failing code, applies a precise patch, runs the specific migration tests to verify the fix, and summarizes the change clearly. Transcript 2 is more verbose, dumps large swaths of code unnecessarily, and doesn’t demonstrate post-patch verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep understanding of Sphinx’s signature‐parsing machinery, pinpoints the root cause in signature_from_str, crafts and tests a precise patch, and verifies it with both unit tests and manual checks. Transcript 2, in contrast, largely just lists files and greps without producing a coherent, working fix.

Transcript 2 is concise and presents a clear plan, correctly identifies the root cause in signature_from_str, provides a focused patch, and verifies the fix with targeted tests. Transcript 1 is long and meanders through failed patches and test failures without arriving at a clean solution.

Transcript 1 shows a focused, successful patch: it identifies the bug, applies a minimal code change (using rsplit), adds a dedicated test, and verifies all tests pass, then summarizes concisely. Transcript 2 is much more verbose, includes many failed patch attempts, and ends with broken tests. Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 delivers a clear, concise plan, pinpoints the right code location in docfields.py, applies the minimal patch (split→rsplit), adds a targeted test with a minimal Sphinx project, and summarizes the change. Transcript 1 is verbose, struggles with tooling, and never cleanly completes the fix.

Transcript 1 concisely identifies the root cause in sphinx.util.inspect.object_description and applies a minimal, correct patch that passes all tests. Transcript 2, by contrast, wanders through unrelated code paths, repeatedly fails to apply the patch cleanly, and breaks a host of unrelated tests. This shows Transcript 1 came from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 gives a concise, correct patch that special-cases enum.Enum in object_description(), explains exactly why it works, demonstrates a quick manual verification, and notes no regressions—all without getting lost in low-level patch failures. Transcript 1 is overly verbose, fumbles patch application, and ends with broken tests.

Transcript 1 systematically implements a full linear‐Gaussian structure learning pipeline from scratch—handling missing libraries, coding OLS with Gaussian elimination, BIC scoring, greedy edge selection with tie‐breaking, parameter fitting, intervention, and sampling—demonstrating depth and robustness. Transcript 2 resorts to heuristic correlation and partial‐correlation analysis and manual DAG specification.

Transcript 2 uses a systematic, BIC‐scored greedy structure learning algorithm with proper acyclicity checks, tie‐breaking rules, and a clear planning framework, whereas Transcript 1 relies on ad hoc correlation thresholds and manual edge assignments. The second transcript demonstrates more robust, generalizable code and better handles the constraints and scoring.

Transcript 2 uses a concise high-level Python meet-in-the-middle, derives and tests the inverse F function cleanly, and completes the key recovery and decryption in fewer lines without verbose C boilerplate and manual patching. Its solution is more elegant and efficient, indicating the more capable model.

Transcript 1 shows a clear, high-level strategy (analytically inverting the F-function, building a meet-in-the-middle in Python) and working code on the first try, whereas Transcript 2 flails with solver availability, resorts to unwieldy C boilerplate, and even needs manual patching. The systematic, correct, and concise approach in Transcript 1 indicates the more capable model.

Transcript 1 shows a clear, systematic strategy: it defines a shared set of 8 shapes by quantiles across both buckets, implements adaptive gen_len binning, tunes parameters until all thresholds are met, and presents a concise summary. Transcript 2 is far more ad-hoc, with repeated trial-and-error, struggled importing the cost model, and lacked the same coherence and targeted optimization.

Transcript 2 demonstrates clear high-level planning, structured iterative refinement, and concise summarization of strategy and results, whereas Transcript 1 is a more ad-hoc, brute-force exploration without an explicit plan. Transcript 2’s coherent design and explanation indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a clear, structured plan with robust error handling, minimal repetition, and a sophisticated implementation of the mapping algorithm. It cleanly initializes the environment, fetches and merges bundles with proper conflict resolution, and dynamically verifies the solution against all examples. Transcript 2 is disorganized, with repeated package installs, trial-and-error commands, and less coherent conflict resolution. Therefore, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper algorithmic insight and produces a clear, efficient, well-documented implementation for deducing the minimal repeating period, while Transcript 2 falls back to a brute-force permutation approach and less robust logic. The quality and generality of the solution in Transcript 1 indicate it came from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 shows a clear, structured approach with detailed subpattern design, boundary checks, and explicit handling of the “last date” requirement, along with testing (even if the tool was unavailable) and a concise summary. Transcript 2 is more ad-hoc, with failed tool calls and minimal explanation.

Transcript 2 shows a clear multi-step plan, careful composition of subpatterns, sample-based validation (and proper handling when the test tool fails), and a concise summary of the final regex along with usage notes. Transcript 1 is more tangled and repetitive without structured reasoning or testing.

Transcript 1 demonstrates systematic planning, clear step tracking with concise ontology discovery, efficient use of FILTER/VALUES for EU codes, and a well-structured nested subquery for the student count. Transcript 2, while correct, is more verbose and repetitive in data inspection and lacks the same level of planning rigor.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a clear, structured planning approach, efficiently inspects the ontology, and produces a concise, well-justified SPARQL query with correct use of FILTER EXISTS and subqueries. It avoids unnecessary repetition and follows a logical plan, indicating higher capability.
